question: You have driven for many hours and your eyes keep closing at traffic lights. What should you do?
optionA: Stop work and rest
optionB: Open the windows wide and carry on driving
optionC: Drink a strong coffee and take one more job
optionD: Turn up the radio and drive more slowly
explanation: Fatigue slows your reactions as much as alcohol. Fresh air, coffee or music only mask it for minutes; the only fix is to stop and rest.

question: A passenger in the back seat has not buckled up. What should you do before moving off?
optionA: Drive off, as it is their choice
optionB: Politely ask them to wear the belt
optionC: Wait until you reach the expressway
optionD: Remind them only if police are near
explanation: Everyone in the car must wear a seat belt where one is fitted. A short, polite reminder before moving off protects the passenger and you.

question: You stop at the kerb to let a passenger out on the right side of the car. What is the main danger?
optionA: The meter running on a little longer than usual
optionB: The passenger forgetting to take a receipt
optionC: A pedestrian walking on the left footway
optionD: A rider passing on that side
explanation: A door opened into traffic can hit a cyclist, PMD user or motorcyclist. Ask passengers to get out on the kerb side and check before any door opens.

question: Before a passenger opens a door, what is the safest habit for you as the driver?
optionA: Check mirrors and blind spot first
optionB: Unlock all doors as you brake
optionC: Tell them to open the door quickly
optionD: Switch on the interior light only
explanation: Checking the mirrors and over your shoulder before doors open catches cyclists and riders coming up alongside. Keep the doors locked until it is clear.

question: A booking app pings with a new job while you are driving. What should you do?
optionA: Ignore it until you can stop safely
optionB: Accept it quickly at the next junction
optionC: Hold the phone low and tap accept
optionD: Ask the passenger to accept it for you
explanation: Handling a phone while the car moves is an offence and a common cause of crashes. Set the app up before you move and deal with jobs only when parked safely.

question: Where should a phone used for navigation be placed while you drive?
optionA: On your lap, within easy reach of your hand
optionB: On the passenger seat beside you
optionD: In your hand, held below the windscreen
explanation: A mounted phone set up before the trip lets you glance at directions without holding it. Programme the route while stationary.

question: It starts raining heavily on the PIE. How should you change your driving?
optionA: Keep the speed but brake earlier
optionB: Switch on the hazard lights and carry on
optionC: Slow down and double the gap ahead
optionD: Move into the right lane to overtake
explanation: Wet roads lengthen stopping distances and cut visibility. Drop your speed, leave a much bigger gap and use headlights, not hazard lights, while moving.

question: When are hazard warning lights correctly used?
optionA: When stopped as an obstruction
optionB: When driving slowly through heavy rain
optionC: When parking briefly on a double yellow line
optionD: When thanking a driver who gave way
explanation: Hazard lights warn others that your stationary vehicle is an obstruction, such as after a breakdown. They are not a licence to stop where stopping is not allowed.

question: A passenger says they are late and asks you to speed. What should you do?
optionA: Speed up on quiet stretches only
optionB: Take a bus lane to save time
optionC: Jump the amber lights to help them
optionD: Keep to the limit and explain why
explanation: Your licence, your passenger's safety and other road users come first. Keep to the speed limit and tell the passenger calmly that you will get them there safely.

question: You are approaching a signalised crossing as the light turns amber and you could stop safely. What should you do?
optionA: Speed up to clear the junction
optionB: Sound the horn and continue
explanation: Amber means stop unless you are so close that stopping would be unsafe. Rushing an amber light is how red-light crashes happen.

question: You pass a 'Start of silver zone' sign with a speed limit sign attached. What does it tell you?
optionA: A hospital entrance is on the left side
optionB: Cyclists may use the whole lane ahead
optionC: Only taxis may stop for older passengers
optionD: Watch for elderly pedestrians; keep to the limit
explanation: Silver Zones are in estates with many seniors. Slow down, look out for elderly pedestrians crossing and do not exceed the posted speed limit.

question: Children are near a school during dismissal time. How should you drive past?
optionA: At the normal limit, using the horn
optionB: In the right lane to keep away
optionC: Slowly, ready to stop for a child
explanation: Children can dart out from between parked cars. In a school zone keep to the lower limit, cover the brake and watch the kerbs.

question: A cyclist is riding ahead of you in your lane on a narrow road. How should you pass?
optionA: Sound the horn so they move aside
optionB: Squeeze past close to the kerb
optionC: Wait, then pass with a wide gap
optionD: Follow closely until they turn off
explanation: Give a cyclist plenty of space and pass only when it is safe to do so. A horn can startle a rider into a fall.

question: When is your blind spot most likely to hide a motorcyclist?
optionA: When you stop at a red light
optionB: When you change lanes
optionC: When you reverse into a driveway
optionD: When you drive straight ahead slowly
explanation: Motorcycles fit easily into the area your mirrors do not show. A shoulder check before every lane change finds them.

question: After a long day, how can you best plan your shifts to avoid fatigue?
optionA: Take regular breaks and enough sleep
optionB: Drive until the evening peak is over
optionC: Finish every shift with a night job
optionD: Rely on energy drinks between jobs
explanation: Planned breaks and proper sleep are what prevent fatigue. Stimulants wear off suddenly and leave you more tired.

question: You have taken medicine that says it may cause drowsiness. What should you do?
optionA: Drive, but use only the expressways
optionB: Drive, but keep the windows open for air
optionC: Not drive until it wears off
optionD: Take passengers on short trips only
explanation: Drowsy medicine affects judgement and reaction time just as fatigue does. Check the label and ask your doctor or pharmacist before you work.

question: A passenger wants you to stop right at a busy junction to get out. What should you do?
optionA: Stop at once to avoid an argument
optionB: Stop on the pedestrian crossing
optionC: Stop in the yellow box briefly
optionD: Stop further on, where it is safe
explanation: Junctions, crossings and yellow boxes are dangerous and usually illegal places to stop. Explain and pull in at the next safe spot.

question: Your engine warning light comes on mid-trip and the car loses power. What is the safest action?
optionA: Pull over safely and get help
optionB: Finish the trip first, then check it
optionC: Drive faster to reach the depot before it fails
optionD: Ignore it while the car still moves
explanation: A fault that cuts power can leave you stranded in a dangerous place. Stop where it is safe, put the hazard lights on and arrange help and another vehicle for the passenger.

question: Which daily check helps keep your taxi or private hire car safe?
optionA: Radio, mats and air freshener
optionB: Meter tariff and receipt roll only
explanation: A quick check of tyres, lights, brakes, wipers and fluids before a shift catches faults before they cause a crash.

question: Your tyre tread looks very worn. Why should you change the tyre before your next shift?
optionA: The car will fail its emissions test
optionB: It makes the meter run faster
optionD: Grip falls sharply on wet roads
explanation: Worn tread cannot clear water, so the car can aquaplane and take much longer to stop in Singapore's heavy rain.

question: You are driving at night. When should you dip your headlights?
optionA: Only when driving on the expressways
optionB: When meeting oncoming traffic
optionC: Only when it is raining heavily
optionD: When the street lights are switched off
explanation: High beam dazzles oncoming drivers and those you follow. Dip your lights whenever another road user could be blinded.

question: A passenger who has been drinking tries to grab the steering wheel. What should you do?
optionA: Speed up to reach the address
optionB: Stop safely and ask them to stop
optionC: Push their hand away while driving
explanation: Interference with the driver is dangerous. Pull over where it is safe, stay calm and call the police if the passenger will not stop.

question: A person on a personal mobility device is on the road beside your car. What should you expect?
optionA: Sudden moves and low speed
optionB: Use of the expressway shoulder
optionC: The same speed as a motorcycle
explanation: Give vulnerable road users plenty of room. A small device rider is slow and can swerve without warning, so hold back and pass only with a wide gap.

question: You need to reverse out of a driveway at a condominium. What makes it safer?
optionA: Reverse slowly, looking all round
optionB: Reverse quickly to clear the gate before cars come
optionC: Rely only on the rear camera screen
optionD: Ask the passenger to watch behind for you
explanation: Cameras and sensors help, but children and pedestrians can appear fast. Move slowly and keep looking all round, and get out to check if unsure.

question: Your car starts to aquaplane on a wet road. What should you do?
optionA: Brake hard and hold the pedal down
optionB: Steer sharply towards the kerb
optionD: Accelerate to push through the water
explanation: Aquaplaning takes away steering control and braking efficiency. Slow down by braking intermittently (on/off) until you regain control.

question: What gap does the Traffic Police handbook recommend behind the car ahead?
optionA: At least one second
optionB: At least three seconds
optionC: One car length at any speed
explanation: The Basic Theory of Driving uses the 'three-second' rule (previously two seconds): count three seconds from when the car ahead passes a fixed object.

question: You are tired and a passenger asks for a long trip to Tuas. What is the right choice?
optionA: Accept it and drive with all the windows down
optionB: Decline it if you are unfit to drive
optionC: Accept it and rest on the expressway shoulder
optionD: Accept it but skip the vehicle checks
explanation: Refusing a hire without a reasonable excuse is an offence, but being unfit to drive safely is a real safety reason. Do not start a trip you cannot finish safely.

question: A motorcycle is filtering between lanes as traffic slows. What should you do?
optionA: Close the gap in front to block it
optionB: Move over quickly into the next lane to let it by
optionC: Flash your headlights to warn it off
explanation: Motorcycles move through slow traffic. Hold your lane, signal early and check your mirrors before any move.

question: You feel angry after a rude driver cuts in front of you. What is the safest response?
optionA: Follow closely to show displeasure
optionB: Let it go and keep a safe gap
optionD: Sound the horn for a long time
explanation: Retaliating turns a near miss into road rage. Let the other driver go and keep your attention on your passenger and the road.

question: Where is the safest place to set down a passenger on a busy road?
optionA: The middle lane at a red light
optionB: Beside a bus stop on the kerb
optionC: A taxi stand, stop or driveway
explanation: Designated taxi stands, taxi stops and building driveways are the safest places for passengers to get in and out.

question: Your passenger wants to get out while you wait in a traffic jam in the second lane. What should you do?
optionA: Unlock the doors so they can walk across
optionB: Wait until you reach the kerb
optionC: Tell them to use the right-hand door instead
optionD: Let them out if no bus is near
explanation: Getting out in a live traffic lane puts the passenger between moving vehicles. Move to the kerb or a safe stopping place first.

question: A passenger in the back asks you to put their bag on the front passenger seat. What should you consider?
optionA: The bag might block the view of the meter
optionB: It adds a luggage charge to the booking fee
optionC: It could fly forward if you brake hard
explanation: Loose items become missiles in a sudden stop. Put heavy items in the boot or secure them.

question: A passenger gets into your taxi. What should you do first?
optionA: Start driving towards the city straight away
optionB: Greet them and confirm the destination
optionC: Ask how they plan to pay
optionD: Ask which app they usually use
explanation: A greeting and a quick check of the destination start the trip well and avoid wrong-address disputes later.

question: A passenger names a road you do not know. What is the best response?
optionA: Say so and agree the route
optionB: Guess and correct the route later on
optionC: Drive towards town and ask again there
optionD: Ask them to take another taxi
explanation: Being honest and agreeing the route, using a map or app, avoids a dispute over the fare and the way taken.

question: A passenger disputes the fare at the end of a trip. How should you handle it?
optionA: Lock the doors until they pay
optionB: Raise your voice so they back down
optionC: Stay calm and explain the charges
explanation: Explain the meter or app fare and any surcharges politely. If it cannot be settled, record the details and let the operator or the authorities deal with it.

question: A passenger shouts at you because of heavy traffic. What should you do?
optionA: Shout back so that they calm down
optionB: Stop and order them out of the car
optionC: Stay polite and keep driving safely
explanation: Staying calm and courteous usually defuses anger. Ending the hire without a reasonable excuse before the destination is an offence.

question: Which remark to a passenger could lead to demerit points?
optionA: A polite question about the route
optionB: An insulting or harassing comment
optionC: A request to fasten the seat belt
optionD: A reminder about the fare shown
explanation: Verbally insulting, intimidating or harassing a passenger is an offence under the vocational licence rules and carries demerit points.

question: A passenger is talking on the phone and seems busy. How should you treat conversation?
optionA: Ask personal questions to be friendly
optionB: Keep it brief and let them lead
explanation: Good service means reading the passenger. Some like to chat; many want quiet. Never ask intrusive personal questions.

question: You find a wallet on the back seat after a passenger leaves. What must you do?
optionA: Keep it until someone calls you about it
optionB: Post a photo of it online to find the owner
optionC: Give it to the next passenger
optionD: Hand it in as the rules require
explanation: Property left in the vehicle must be deposited as the rules require. Holding it for more than 24 hours, and especially for seven days or more, brings demerit points.

question: A passenger calls about a phone they left in your car. What should you do?
optionA: Ask for a reward before saying anything
optionB: Say you did not see a phone in the car
optionC: Help them get it back properly
optionD: Keep it if they were rude to you
explanation: Help the passenger recover their property, following your operator's lost property process and the rules on depositing it.

question: A passenger asks you to wait while they run into a shop. What should you make clear?
optionA: That waiting is never allowed
optionB: That they must leave a deposit
optionC: That you will leave after a minute
explanation: On a metered trip, waiting time is charged by the meter. Telling the passenger first avoids a dispute later.

question: A passenger is visibly drunk and unsteady. What is the best approach?
optionA: Be patient and get them home safely
optionB: Refuse the hire at once without any reason
optionC: Leave them at the roadside halfway there
explanation: A drunk passenger still needs a safe trip. Stay calm and polite; if they become violent or abusive, stop safely and call the police.

question: A passenger tells you they feel threatened by someone following them. What should you do?
optionA: Go to a safe place; offer to call 999
optionB: Tell them it is not your problem to solve
optionC: Drop them at the nearest street corner
optionD: Drive faster, even through red lights
explanation: Your role is to keep the passenger safe within the law. A busy, well-lit place and a call to 999 are the right steps.

question: A passenger asks you to switch off the air-conditioning. What should you do?
optionA: Refuse, as you set the cabin
optionB: Adjust it to their comfort
optionC: Ask them to pay extra for it
optionD: Switch it off and open all windows
explanation: Within reason, the cabin temperature should suit the passenger. Small comforts shape how they rate the trip.

question: Your passenger leaves a negative comment about your driving. How should you respond?
optionA: Find their home address
optionB: Message them to argue
explanation: Feedback helps you improve. Contacting a passenger to argue, or using their details for anything outside the trip, is unprofessional and may break the law.

question: A passenger asks for your personal number to book you directly next time. What should you consider?
optionA: Bookings must follow your licence rules
optionB: Any private deal with a passenger is allowed
optionC: Only cash jobs need to go through an app
optionD: Taxis may not take repeat customers
explanation: A private hire car may only take passengers on a booking made through a licensed or licence-exempt operator. Street pick-ups and touting are offences.

question: Your passenger wants to bring an open durian into the car. What is a fair response?
optionA: Shout at them and drive away
optionB: Charge a cleaning fee on the spot in cash
optionC: Explain politely and suggest sealing it
optionD: Throw the fruit out of the window
explanation: Explain calmly why a strong-smelling item is a problem, and look for a fair solution such as sealing it in a bag, rather than an argument.

question: A family has more passengers than your car has seat belts. What should you do?
optionA: Let a child sit on an adult's lap
optionB: Put one passenger in the boot
optionC: Take only as many as there are seats
optionD: Take them all if the trip is short
explanation: Carrying more passengers than seats is unsafe and breaks the rules. Help them book a larger vehicle.

question: A passenger asks you to take a different route from the one your app shows. What should you do?
optionA: Insist on the route the app shows
optionB: Stop the trip there and ask them out
optionC: Take the longest route to teach them
optionD: Follow it if it is safe and legal
explanation: The passenger may choose the route. Confirm it so there is no argument about the fare later.

question: Which personal habit most affects a passenger's comfort?
optionA: Loud music that you enjoy
optionB: Eating your lunch while driving
explanation: A tidy car and a neat, clean appearance show professionalism. Loud music, eating and strong scents bother many passengers.

question: A passenger is crying quietly in the back seat. What is the most respectful response?
optionA: Ask what happened to them in detail
optionB: Post about it on social media later
explanation: Respect the passenger's privacy. You can gently ask if they are all right, but do not pry.

question: A passenger asks you to stop the meter and accept a lump sum instead. What should you do?
optionA: Agree if they pay the whole amount in cash
optionB: Agree for trips to the airport
optionC: Agree if no one finds out
optionD: Decline and keep the meter on
explanation: Street-hail taxi fares are charged by the meter. Demanding or taking a fare outside the pricing policy is an offence that carries demerit points.

question: A passenger starts filming you with their phone during an argument. How should you respond?
optionA: Grab the phone from them
optionB: Film them back and post it
explanation: Calm, professional behaviour protects you. A recording of you staying courteous is the best record of the event.

question: A passenger lights a cigarette in your car. What should you do?
optionA: Ignore it to keep the peace
optionB: Ask them politely to stop
explanation: Smoking is prohibited in taxis, and in private hire cars on paid chauffeured service since 1 October 2017. Ask politely; if they refuse, stop at a safe place and seek help.

question: Your passenger is a tourist who speaks little English. What helps most?
optionA: Speak louder and faster in English
optionB: Confirm it on a map
optionC: Guess which hotel they probably mean
explanation: Showing the address on a phone map or the booking screen avoids taking a tourist to the wrong place.

question: At the end of a trip, what should you remind passengers to do?
optionA: Check for their belongings
optionB: Rate you five stars in the app
optionD: Close all the windows before leaving
explanation: A quick reminder to check for phones, bags and wallets prevents most lost property.

question: A passenger asks you to drive while they sleep and wake them on arrival. What should you do?
optionA: Drive smoothly and wake them gently
optionB: Take a longer route while they sleep
optionD: Leave them asleep at the kerb
explanation: A sleeping passenger relies on your honesty. Take the agreed or most direct route and wake them politely at the destination.

question: A passenger tries to talk politics and you disagree strongly. What is professional?
optionA: Argue the point until they agree
optionB: Stay neutral and politely move on
explanation: Keeping the conversation neutral and courteous avoids conflict. Your job is a safe, pleasant trip.

question: Why should you keep a record when a passenger becomes violent?
optionA: To give facts to police and operator
optionB: To post the whole story online
optionC: To refuse them on future trips only
optionD: To claim a higher fare for the trip
explanation: Writing down the time, place and what happened helps the police and your operator deal with the incident.

question: A passenger asks you to help lift a heavy suitcase into the boot. What should you do?
optionA: Help, lifting safely
optionB: Refuse, as luggage is the passenger's job
optionC: Charge a separate fee for it
optionD: Put it on the back seat unsecured
explanation: Helping with luggage is part of good service. Bend your knees and keep the load close to avoid injury.

question: A passenger asks you to stop at a petrol station toilet on a long trip. What is reasonable?
optionA: Refuse and keep driving to the address
optionB: End the trip there
optionC: Leave them and take another job
optionD: Stop safely and wait for them
explanation: Reasonable requests should be met where safe. The trip continues once they return.

question: A passenger offers you a tip. What is correct?
optionA: Demand one on every trip you make
optionB: Add it to the meter reading
optionC: Thank them; never ask for one
explanation: Tips are voluntary. Keeping change or pressing a passenger for money harms trust and may break the fare rules.

question: A passenger compliments you and asks for your name for the operator. What should you do?
optionA: Give them a made-up name
optionB: Refuse, as names are secret
explanation: Your identification is displayed so passengers can identify you. They can use it to give feedback through the operator.

question: Two passengers start fighting in the back seat. What should you do?
optionA: Keep driving to the destination quickly
optionB: Stop safely and call the police
explanation: A fight in the car is dangerous for everyone. Pull over where it is safe, get out if needed and call 999.

question: A wheelchair user books your car and uses a folding wheelchair. What should you do?
optionA: Lift them into the car without asking first
optionB: Tell them to fold it themselves
optionC: Ask how they want help, then stow it
explanation: Ask first: the passenger knows how best to transfer and how the chair folds. Then store it carefully in the boot.

question: You see a road sign showing white walking sticks. What should you do?
optionA: Sound the horn to warn the pedestrians ahead
optionB: Keep your speed, as it marks a footpath only
optionC: Stop only if a police officer is present
optionD: Slow down; stop for blind people crossing
explanation: The white walking sticks sign warns of blind pedestrians. Slow down and stop if necessary to give way to blind people crossing the road.

question: You arrive for a booked passenger who is blind and waiting at the kerb. What should you do first?
optionA: Say who you are and name the booking
optionB: Sound the horn twice and wait
optionD: Wait in the car until they find you
explanation: A horn or headlights mean nothing to someone who cannot see you. Walk over, introduce yourself, confirm the booking and offer your arm to the door.

question: You arrive at the destination of a passenger who cannot see. What should you do?
optionA: Stop and wait in silence for them to move
optionB: Unlock the doors without speaking
optionD: Say you have arrived and where
explanation: Tell the passenger you have arrived, which side to get out on and what is around, such as a step or a kerb.

question: A passenger who is deaf gives you a written address. How should you communicate?
optionA: Shout so that they can hear you
optionB: Talk while looking ahead at the road
optionC: Face them; use writing or a phone
explanation: Many deaf people lip-read. Face them, speak clearly or type on a phone, and confirm the destination in writing.

question: An elderly passenger takes a long time to get into the car. What should you do?
optionA: Sound the horn to hurry them up
optionB: Be patient and offer help
optionD: Drive off before they settle in
explanation: Older passengers may need time and a steady hand. Patience is part of the service and keeps them safe.

question: A passenger with dementia seems confused about where they live. What should you do?
optionA: Drop them at any nearby HDB block
optionB: Stay calm and contact a carer or police
optionC: Tell them to get out and walk home
explanation: Look for a contact card or ask gently. If you cannot find a safe destination, contact a family member, carer or the police.

question: Which seat is usually easiest for a passenger with limited mobility?
optionA: The middle rear seat
optionB: The rear seat directly behind you
optionD: Any seat, it makes no difference
explanation: A front seat moved back gives most room to swing the legs in, but always ask the passenger what works for them.

question: A private hire car passenger is travelling with a child shorter than 1.35 m. What must the car provide?
optionA: A booster seat or child restraint
optionB: Nothing, as long as the trip is short
optionD: A cushion placed under the child
explanation: Private hire cars must provide booster seats or child restraints for passengers below 1.35 m in height, whatever their age.

question: When must a private hire car provide a child restraint for a passenger under 1.35 m?
optionA: Whatever the child's age
optionB: Only for children under 3
explanation: The rule for private hire cars is set by height, not age: anyone under 1.35 m needs a booster seat or child restraint.

question: A passenger uses a walking frame. What helps them most?
optionA: In the middle lane at the lights
optionB: Close to the kerb, on level ground
optionC: On a slope, to save time
explanation: A level stop close to the kerb and entrance makes getting in and out much safer.

question: A passenger with an intellectual disability is travelling alone. How should you speak to them?
optionA: As you would speak to a small child
optionB: Only to their carer, by phone
optionC: Loudly and slowly in every word
optionD: Plainly, as you would any adult
explanation: Use clear, simple words and treat the passenger with the same respect as any adult.

question: A wheelchair user asks if your vehicle can take their motorised chair. It cannot. What should you do?
optionA: Try to force it into the boot anyway
optionB: Tell them they should not travel
optionD: Explain and help book a suitable car
explanation: Heavy motorised chairs need a wheelchair-accessible vehicle. Be honest and help them find one.

question: A pregnant passenger asks you to drive gently. What should you do?
optionA: Take the fastest route at higher speed
optionB: Ask her to move to the front seat
explanation: Smooth acceleration and braking make the ride more comfortable and safe.

question: A passenger has a hidden disability and asks for quiet. What should you do?
optionA: Ask them to prove the condition first
optionB: Keep the radio on loud
optionD: Charge extra for the special request
explanation: Not every disability can be seen. Respect reasonable requests without asking for explanations.

question: An older passenger pays with cash and counts slowly. What is good practice?
optionA: Wait and count the change back
optionB: Take the purse and count it yourself
optionC: Round the fare up for the time taken
optionD: Rush them out of the car
explanation: Never handle a passenger's purse. Wait, count the change back clearly and thank them.

question: A child aged about ten is alone, waiting to be picked up by a booked car. What should you check?
optionA: Nothing, children travel the same as adults
optionB: That the child can pay with cash
optionC: That the child sits in the front seat
explanation: Make sure the booking is genuine and that an adult at the destination is expected. If something seems wrong, contact the operator.

question: A passenger with a stoma bag asks you to avoid sudden bumps. What should you do?
optionA: Drive smoothly on an even route
optionB: Say it is not your problem to solve
optionC: Drive faster to finish the trip sooner
explanation: Small adjustments in driving style help passengers with medical needs travel in comfort.

question: A passenger uses sign language with a friend. What should you avoid?
optionA: Waiting for them to finish
optionB: Staring or commenting on it
explanation: Treat sign language like any other private conversation.

question: A passenger who is blind wants to pay by card. How can you help?
optionA: Take their card and ask for their PIN
optionB: Say the amount; guide them to the reader
optionC: Ask a bystander to pay for them
explanation: Say the fare clearly and guide their hand to the card reader. Never ask for their PIN.

question: Which vehicles may the holder of a Taxi Driver's Vocational Licence (TDVL) drive for hire?
optionA: Taxis and private hire cars
optionB: Taxis only, and no other vehicle
explanation: A TDVL lets you drive a taxi and also a private hire car. A PDVL covers private hire cars only.

question: Which vehicle may the holder of a PDVL drive for hire?
optionA: A taxi or a private hire car
optionB: A private hire car only
optionC: A taxi only, not a private hire car
explanation: The Private Hire Car Driver's Vocational Licence covers private hire cars. Driving a taxi needs a TDVL.

question: A PDVL holder wants to start driving a taxi. What must they do?
optionA: Nothing, the PDVL already covers taxis
optionB: Convert the PDVL to a TDVL
optionC: Register with a taxi company only
optionD: Fix taxi decals to their car
explanation: Driving a taxi needs a TDVL. A PDVL holder can convert through LTA's PDVL to TDVL conversion route.

question: A PDVL is converted to a TDVL. How long is the new TDVL valid?
optionA: For three years from the conversion
optionB: For the rest of the PDVL's term
optionC: For one year from the conversion
explanation: A TDVL obtained by conversion runs only for the remaining validity of the original PDVL.

question: For how long is a renewed TDVL or PDVL normally valid?
optionA: One year
optionB: Three years
explanation: Vocational licences are renewed for three years. Holders aged 67 and above may get a shorter period.

question: How often must a vocational licence holder attend refresher training?
optionA: Once every six years
optionB: Every year
explanation: Taxi and private hire drivers attend a refresher course once every six years from the date the licence was issued.

question: A TDVL holder has a good demerit record and drives actively. Which refresher course applies?
optionA: The 5-hour course for all holders
optionB: A full 16-hour course again
explanation: Active taxi drivers with a good Vocational Licence Points System record take the 3-hour refresher; other TDVL holders take a 5-hour one.

question: From what age must a vocational licence holder be certified medically fit before each renewal?
explanation: Holders aged 50 and above need regular medical check-ups and must be certified fit to drive a public service vehicle before renewal.

question: At which birthdays must an older taxi or private hire driver pass an on-road Assessment of Fitness to Drive to keep the licence?
explanation: Holders turning 70, 73 and 74 must pass an on-road assessment in addition to the medical requirements.

question: What is the statutory age limit for holding a vocational licence to drive a taxi or private hire car?
explanation: Public service vehicle drivers may hold a vocational licence only up to the statutory age limit of 75.

question: A driver's ordinary driving licence is suspended for 18 months. What happens to the vocational licence?
optionA: It is revoked
optionB: It continues unaffected
explanation: A vocational licence is revoked when the holder's driving licence is disqualified or suspended for one year or more.

question: What type of driving licence must a TDVL or PDVL holder keep valid?
optionA: Singapore class 2B only
optionB: Singapore class 4 or 5
explanation: Vocational licences for taxi and private hire car drivers are built on a valid Singapore class 3 or 3A driving licence.

question: Another driver asks to borrow your vocational licence for a shift. What is the consequence of agreeing?
optionA: A warning letter, with no points
optionB: 21 demerit points
optionD: No penalty if no fare is taken
explanation: Permitting another person to use your vocational licence carries 21 demerit points, enough on its own to lead to revocation.

question: A driver is caught using a friend's vocational licence. What does this offence carry?
optionA: Demerit points under the VLPS
optionB: Nothing, if the friend agreed
optionD: Only a fine for the friend
explanation: Using, wearing or having another person's vocational licence is a scheduled offence that carries demerit points.

question: An LTA officer asks to see your vocational licence while you work. What must you do?
optionA: Show it within 30 days
optionB: Refer them to your operator
explanation: Failing to produce your vocational licence when an authorised officer asks is an offence.

question: Your vocational licence is suspended. What must you do with it?
optionA: Surrender it as required
optionB: Keep driving until it expires
explanation: Failing to surrender a vocational licence on suspension or cancellation is an offence that carries demerit points.

question: A driver's vocational licence expired 4 years ago. How can they drive for hire again?
optionA: Renew it online at once
optionB: Make a new application
explanation: A licence expired for more than three years cannot be renewed; the driver must apply afresh.

question: A licence expired two months ago. What is the usual route?
optionA: Make a full new application from scratch
optionB: Take a conversion course
optionD: Renew it in the usual way
explanation: A licence that expired less than six months ago can still be renewed through the normal channels.

question: Driving a taxi with an expired vocational licence carries how many demerit points?
explanation: Driving a chauffeured private hire car or taxi with an expired vocational licence is a 21-point scheduled offence.

question: What must self-employed taxi and private hire drivers be up to date with to renew their licence?
optionA: MediSave contributions
optionB: Road tax for every car they drive
explanation: Self-employed applicants must have paid their MediSave contributions in full or be on an active GIRO arrangement with CPF.

question: You convert your car out of the private hire car scheme. What happens to your PDVL?
optionA: It is cancelled on the day of conversion
optionB: It turns into a TDVL
optionD: It is suspended for a month
explanation: Converting the vehicle out of the scheme does not affect the remaining validity of a TDVL or PDVL.

question: What must you have before using a chauffeured private hire car for paid trips?
optionA: Only a class 3 licence held for a year
optionB: Only a taxi company badge
optionD: A valid PDVL or TDVL and insurance
explanation: Drivers providing paid point-to-point trips in a chauffeured private hire car must hold a valid PDVL or TDVL and adequate motor insurance.

question: A vocational licence holder is convicted in court of a serious offence. What can happen?
optionA: Nothing, as vocational licences last for life
optionB: Only a refresher course is needed
explanation: A licence cannot be renewed after a court conviction, and convictions can lead to revocation.

question: A driver was first granted a vocational licence in 2025. In what form is it issued?
optionA: A paper certificate only
optionB: A metal badge only
explanation: Drivers licensed on or after 1 April 2023 receive a digital LTA vocational licence instead of a physical card.

question: Which drivers are covered by the Vocational Licence Points System (VLPS)?
optionA: Taxi drivers only, not private hire drivers
optionB: All class 3 licence holders
explanation: The VLPS applies to holders of vocational licences for taxis and chauffeured private hire cars.

question: When are VLPS demerit points awarded for a scheduled offence?
optionA: On conviction or composition
optionB: Only after a conviction in court
optionD: Only if a passenger complains twice
explanation: Points are awarded when the holder is convicted of a scheduled offence or pays a composition sum to settle it.

question: Over what period are VLPS demerit points added up to decide a suspension?
optionA: Any 24 months
optionB: Any 12 months
explanation: The relevant period is any 24 months ending on the date of the latest offence.

question: A driver collects 8 VLPS demerit points within 24 months. What suspension may follow?
optionA: No suspension
optionB: 4 weeks
explanation: A total of 6 to 10 points may lead to a 2-week suspension of the vocational licence.

question: A driver collects 13 VLPS points within 24 months. What suspension may follow?
optionA: 2 weeks
optionB: 8 weeks
explanation: A total of 11 to 15 points may lead to a 4-week suspension.

question: A driver collects 18 VLPS points within 24 months. What may happen?
optionA: A 2-week suspension
optionB: A warning letter only
explanation: A total of 16 or more points may lead to an 8-week suspension; more than 20 may lead to revocation.

question: Above how many VLPS points in 24 months may a vocational licence be revoked?
explanation: A vocational licence may be revoked when the holder's points within the relevant period exceed 20.

question: A driver has 4 VLPS points within 24 months. What happens?
optionA: A 2-week suspension
optionB: A 4-week suspension
explanation: Totals of 1 to 5 points do not lead to a suspension, but they count towards later totals.

question: Before LTA suspends or revokes a vocational licence for demerit points, what must it do?
optionA: Seize the car at once without notice
optionB: Give written notice first
explanation: The Registrar must give written notice with at least 14 days for the holder to make written representations before deciding.

question: Which offence carries the most VLPS points?
optionA: Starting the meter before the passenger boards
optionB: Obstructing other taxis at a stand
explanation: Installing or using audio or visual recording equipment in a taxi or private hire car without authority carries 21 points; the meter offences carry 3.

question: A driver shares online a video recorded inside their taxi showing a passenger. What is the consequence?
optionA: 3 demerit points
optionB: A warning only
optionD: No offence if faces are blurred
explanation: Disclosing a visual recording made of any person or incident inside a taxi or private hire car is a 21-point offence.

question: Which of these is a VLPS offence for a taxi driver?
optionA: Asking a passenger to wear a seat belt
optionB: Confirming the destination
explanation: Refusing, without reasonable excuse, to hire out the taxi or convey a passenger carries 6 demerit points.

question: A driver ends a hire halfway and orders the passenger out without a good reason. What follows?
optionA: Demerit points
optionB: Nothing, as long as the meter is stopped
optionC: Only a refund of the fare is due
explanation: Terminating a hire or requiring the passenger to leave, without reasonable excuse, before reaching the destination carries 5 points.

question: How many VLPS points does verbally harassing a passenger in a sexual manner carry?
optionA: 5 demerit points
optionB: 12 demerit points
explanation: Verbally insulting, intimidating or harassing a passenger in a sexual manner is a 5-point offence; LTA's offences list gives 5 points for insulting, intimidating or harassing a passenger in any manner.

question: What does causing hurt to a passenger through careless behaviour bring?
optionA: 21 demerit points
optionB: 5 demerit points
explanation: Causing hurt to a passenger through carelessness or wilful misbehaviour carries 5 points under the VLPS.

question: A driver keeps a passenger's left-behind bag for two days before handing it in. What follows?
optionA: 5 demerit points
optionB: 21 demerit points
explanation: Failing to deposit left property as required for more than 24 hours but less than seven days carries 5 points.

question: A driver holds onto a passenger's lost phone for eight days. How serious is this under the VLPS?
optionA: 3 points
optionB: 5 points
explanation: Keeping left property for seven days or more carries 21 points.

question: Which of these is an offence for a private hire car driver?
optionA: Picking up a passenger who booked
optionB: Soliciting passengers on the street
explanation: Private hire cars must not ply for hire. Soliciting, or loitering to solicit, carries 12 points for a PDVL holder.

question: A taxi driver tampers with the taximeter. How many VLPS points does this carry?
explanation: Tampering with, adjusting or modifying a taximeter is a 21-point offence.

question: A taxi driver covers the face of the taximeter so the passenger cannot see it. What follows?
optionA: 21 demerit points
optionB: No penalty
explanation: Covering or obscuring the taximeter's face carries 5 points.

question: A taxi driver switches on the meter while the hirer is still walking to the car. What is this?
optionA: An offence carrying points
optionB: Allowed, to save waiting time
optionD: Allowed if the fare is small
explanation: The meter may start only once the passenger has boarded and hired the taxi. Starting it earlier carries 3 demerit points.

question: A taxi trip ends. When must the meter be stopped?
optionA: After the passenger pays
optionB: When the next passenger boards
optionC: At the end of the shift
optionD: As soon as the hiring ends
explanation: Failing to stop the taximeter as soon as the hiring ends is an offence carrying 3 points.

question: During a long trip, a driver resets the meter to zero and restarts it. What is this?
optionA: Allowed after the first hour of a trip
optionB: An offence carrying points
optionC: Allowed for trips to the airport
explanation: Resetting the taximeter during a hiring carries 3 demerit points.

question: A taxi driver takes a longer route without reason when the passenger named a destination. What applies?
optionA: Nothing, as drivers may choose any route
optionB: Only a refund to the passenger
optionC: Points only if over 10 km longer
explanation: Failing, without reasonable cause, to take the shortest and most direct route to the named destination carries 3 points.

question: Which item must not obstruct the front windscreen of a taxi or private hire car?
optionA: The tamper-evident private hire decal
optionB: The interior rear-view mirror
explanation: Obstructing or obscuring the front windscreen of a taxi or chauffeured private hire car is a 5-point offence.

question: A driver accepts trips from a ride-hail app that is not licensed or exempt. What is the consequence?
optionA: Nothing, as long as the fare is fair
optionB: Only the app operator is penalised
explanation: Intentionally taking a booking from an unauthorised provider of ride-hail service carries 6 points.

question: A private hire car is driven without its authorised decal on display. How serious is this?
optionA: 3 demerit points
optionB: 21 demerit points
explanation: Driving a chauffeured private hire car without displaying an authorised decal carries 21 points.

question: A private hire car's decal has faded and is hard to read. What is the risk?
optionA: None, as fading is normal wear
optionB: Only a cleaning fee at inspection
explanation: Driving with a decal that is illegible or discoloured by fading carries 12 points. Replace damaged decals promptly.

question: A taxi driver blocks other taxis from picking up passengers. What applies?
optionA: An offence carrying points
optionB: Nothing, it is fair competition
optionC: Only a warning from the operator
explanation: Hindering or obstructing other taxi drivers from picking up passengers carries 3 points.

question: Which statement about composition and demerit points is correct?
optionA: Paying a composition clears the points
optionB: Only court cases bring any points
optionC: Points are given only for crashes
explanation: Whether the offence is compounded or goes to court, the scheduled demerit points are awarded.

question: Why does LTA keep a register of drivers awarded VLPS points?
optionA: To publish driver rankings online
optionB: To track points over time
optionC: To set fares driver by driver
optionD: To choose the colours of taxis
explanation: The Registrar keeps a register of holders with demerit points so totals within the relevant period can be assessed.

question: A taxi driver demands a fare from a street-hail passenger that is above the published fare. What follows?
optionA: Nothing, if the passenger agrees
optionB: Demerit points under the VLPS
explanation: Demanding or taking a fare inconsistent with the published pricing policy is a scheduled offence; the points rise with the amount.

question: Which vehicles may pick up passengers who flag them down on the street?
optionA: Private hire cars only
optionB: Taxis and private hire cars
optionC: Any car with a booking app
explanation: Street-hail is for taxis. A private hire car cannot be hailed on the street and must be booked.

question: How must a private hire car trip be arranged?
optionA: By waving at the driver from the kerb
optionB: Through a licensed or exempt operator
optionD: By a deal with any passer-by
explanation: Private hire car trips must be booked through a licensed ride-hail operator, or a licence-exempt operator with fewer than 800 vehicles.

question: A ride-hail platform has 800 or more vehicles. What does it need?
optionA: Nothing, as apps are not regulated
optionB: A taxi company licence only
explanation: Ride-hail and car-pool operators with 800 or more vehicles on their platforms must hold an operator licence under the Point-to-Point framework.

question: Which law sets up Singapore's point-to-point passenger transport framework?
optionA: The Road Traffic Act 1961, with no other law
optionB: The Land Transport Authority of Singapore Act 1995
optionC: The Private Hire Vehicles and Chauffeurs Ordinance
optionD: The Point-to-Point Passenger Transport Industry Act 2019
explanation: The Point-to-Point Passenger Transport Industry Act 2019 brought in the framework, in force from 2020.

question: A street-hail passenger boards your taxi. How is the fare charged?
optionA: By the taximeter
optionB: By a flat fare you choose
optionD: By the distance on your phone
explanation: A street-hail fare is charged by the meter, plus any applicable surcharges.

question: A passenger books a flat-fare trip through an app. When must the fare be shown?
optionA: Upfront in the app
optionB: At the end of the trip
optionC: Only if the passenger asks to see it
optionD: On the receipt the next day
explanation: Flat fares for taxis and private hire cars must be shown to the passenger in the app before the ride starts.

question: Which of these is one of the main parts of a metered taxi fare?
optionA: The driver's tip
optionB: The parking coupon
explanation: The fare is made up of the flag-down fare, distance and time-based unit fares, surcharges and booking fees.

question: How are peak-period and late-night taxi surcharges usually calculated?
optionA: As a fixed amount for each passenger
optionB: As a charge for each bag
optionC: As a share of the metered fare
explanation: Peak and late-night surcharges are calculated as a percentage of the metered fare.

question: Which of these places can carry a location surcharge on a taxi trip?
optionA: Any HDB void deck
optionB: Changi Airport
explanation: Location surcharges apply at named places and times, such as Changi Airport, Marina Bay Sands and Resorts World Sentosa.

question: Who sets the taxi fares charged by each taxi company?
optionA: The individual driver on each trip
optionB: The passenger
explanation: Fares are set by each taxi company, with LTA and the Public Transport Council keeping some fare aspects standard.

question: A passenger wants to pay by card but your reader is working. What should you do?
optionA: Accept the card payment
optionB: Insist on cash only
optionD: Ask them to pay later by text
explanation: Taxis may accept cash, credit cards, NETS and CEPAS stored-value cards, subject to the devices fitted.

question: A taxi driver collects a booking fee higher than the operator set. What is this?
optionA: Allowed at peak hours
optionB: A VLPS offence
explanation: Collecting, or even attempting to collect, a booking fee above the one set by the provider is a scheduled offence.

question: Where are the tamper-evident decals of a chauffeured private hire car placed?
optionA: Both front doors, near the handles
optionB: On the roof sign
explanation: Chauffeured private hire cars must display a pair of decals on the front and back windscreens.

question: Your private hire car decal is damaged. Within how long must it be replaced at an inspection centre?
optionA: Three calendar days
optionB: One month
explanation: Damaged decals must be replaced at an LTA-Authorised Inspection Centre within three calendar days.

question: You buy a new car to use as a private hire car. What happens to the decals on your old one?
optionA: They move to the new car
optionB: They can be sold to another driver
optionC: They stay valid on any car
optionD: They cannot move to the new car
explanation: Decal serial numbers are tagged to the vehicle number and cannot be transferred. The new car needs its own decals.

question: A car that is not a private hire car shows a private hire decal. What is this?
optionA: An offence
optionB: Allowed if off duty
explanation: It is an offence for a vehicle that is not a chauffeured private hire car to display a private hire car marking.

question: Why must private hire cars display decals at all times?
optionA: So passengers can see the fares
optionB: So they can be identified
optionC: So they can use bus lanes at peak hours
optionD: So they pay less road tax
explanation: Decals help identify private hire cars and support enforcement against unlicensed services and street pick-ups.

question: How often must a chauffeured private hire car undergo periodic inspection?
optionA: Every two years
optionB: Every six months
explanation: Since 1 January 2021 all private hire cars undergo annual inspection.

question: How often must a taxi undergo periodic inspection?
optionA: Every year
optionB: Every two years
explanation: Taxis are inspected once every six months.

question: A car is being converted into a chauffeured private hire car. What must it pass first?
optionA: A taxi meter test
optionB: A noise test only
explanation: Cars converting into the private hire car scheme must pass an inward conversion inspection unless they passed a periodic inspection in the previous three months.

question: A PDVL holder uses their private hire car for a car-pooling trip. Is this allowed?
optionA: Yes, vocational licence holders may
optionB: No, never in a private hire car
optionD: Only with a taxi meter fitted
explanation: Holders of a valid TDVL or PDVL may use a chauffeured private hire car to provide car-pooling trips.

question: A ride-hail passenger is charged more than the fare last published by the operator. Who can be penalised?
optionA: Only the passenger who paid it
optionB: The driver who took the fare
optionC: Nobody, as apps set the prices
explanation: Taking a ride-hail fare above the one last published by the operator is a scheduled offence for the driver.

question: A passenger booked a taxi through an app. Which fare types can the operator offer?
optionA: Only cash fares paid at the end
optionB: Metered, or flat shown upfront
explanation: Ride-hail operators may offer metered trips on taxis or flat fares for taxis and private hire cars.

question: Which agency licenses taxi and private hire drivers and operators in Singapore?
optionA: The Traffic Police
optionB: The Public Utilities Board
explanation: LTA issues vocational licences and administers the point-to-point framework; the Traffic Police enforce road traffic rules.

question: A private hire car passenger asks to be picked up at a taxi stand. What should you do?
optionA: Use the taxi stand, as it is closest
optionB: Wait at the stand with hazards on
optionD: Park in the stand until they come
explanation: Private hire car passengers may not board or alight at taxi stands. Use a pick-up point or building driveway instead.

question: Where may a taxi not stop to pick up or set down passengers?
optionA: At a taxi stand marked with an LTA sign
optionB: At a building driveway
optionD: In a bus lane during its hours
explanation: Taxis cannot stop in bus lanes during operating hours, close to a bus stop, or where signs and lines prohibit stopping.

question: Your passenger asks to be let out right at a bus stop. What should you do?
optionA: Stop in the bus bay briefly if it is empty
optionB: Stop clear of the bus stop
optionC: Stop if no bus is in sight
explanation: Stopping within 9 metres of a bus stop is an offence. Find a safe, legal place nearby.

question: How must a taxi enter a taxi stand where other taxis are waiting?
optionA: Into any empty space you can see
optionB: From the front to save time
explanation: Drivers must drive into a taxi stand from the rear and move into the foremost vacant space until reaching the front.

question: When may a taxi wait at a taxi stand?
optionA: During the driver's meal break
optionB: Only when available for hire
optionC: While off duty for the rest of the day
explanation: Stopping or stationing a taxi at a taxi stand when it cannot be let out for hire is an offence.

question: Within the CBD, which scheme must taxis follow when picking up or setting down passengers?
optionA: The bus lane scheme
optionB: The Silver Zone scheme
explanation: LTA says taxis within the CBD must adhere to the bus lane scheme: no picking up or setting down on a bus lane during its operating hours.

question: Which road is one where taxis must not stop for safety reasons?
optionA: Any HDB estate road
optionB: Any condominium driveway
optionC: Any taxi stop on Orchard Road
explanation: LTA lists roads such as Finlayson Green, High Street, Orchard Link and Esplanade Drive where taxis must not stop.

question: Your passenger asks to get out where double yellow zig-zag lines run along the kerb. What should you do?
optionA: Stop briefly with the hazard lights on
optionB: Stop if no traffic is behind
optionC: Drive on to a legal stop
optionD: Stop for under a minute only
explanation: Double yellow zig-zag lines mean no stopping at any time, not even to let a passenger out.

question: A road has a bus lane that is outside its operating hours right now. May a taxi stop there to set down?
optionA: No, bus lanes are closed to taxis at all times
optionB: Yes, if stopping is not otherwise banned
optionC: Only if a bus is not in sight
optionD: Only with the hazard lights on
explanation: Taxis must not stop in a bus lane during its operating hours. Outside those hours the normal stopping rules for that stretch apply.

question: You stop to wait for a booked passenger. May you leave the driver's seat?
optionA: Yes, for as long as needed
optionB: Yes, to fetch a drink
optionD: Yes, if the engine is running
explanation: Leaving the driver's seat without reasonable cause is an offence under the conduct rules.

question: Which places does LTA call the safest for passengers to board or alight?
optionA: Bus stops and the bus bays beside them
optionB: Taxi stands, stops and driveways
explanation: LTA says designated taxi stands, taxi stops and building driveways are the safest places to board or alight.

question: How can a driver find LTA-designated taxi stands and stops?
optionA: By the LTA sign or a transport app
optionB: By looking for yellow paint only
optionD: They are not marked in any way
explanation: Designated taxi stands and stops carry a specific LTA sign and can be found with the MyTransport.SG app.

question: A taxi driver deliberately blocks other taxis from stopping at a taxi stand. What is this?
optionA: Acceptable at night when stands are busy
optionB: Allowed if first in the queue
explanation: Wilfully obstructing other taxi drivers from stopping or stationing their taxis at a taxi stand carries demerit points.

question: A taxi driver touts for passengers outside a mall entrance. What is this?
optionA: Soliciting, an offence
optionB: Good marketing for the company
explanation: Soliciting for passengers is a scheduled offence for taxi drivers as well as private hire drivers.

question: Your booked passenger is late and the only kerb space has double yellow lines. What should you do?
optionA: Wait there with hazard lights on
optionB: Wait there for up to five minutes
optionC: Move on and wait somewhere legal
optionD: Wait there if you stay in the car
explanation: Double yellow lines allow only the immediate picking up or setting down of passengers. Waiting there counts as parking, so circle round or wait at a legal spot and contact the passenger.

question: A private hire driver waits at an MRT exit calling out to people for rides. What is this?
optionA: Loitering to solicit
optionB: Allowed as long as the app is open
explanation: Loitering for the purpose of soliciting passengers is a 12-point offence for private hire drivers.

question: A passenger names a destination and no route. Which route should you take?
optionA: The one with the least traffic lights
optionB: The shortest and most direct one
optionC: The one you know best, however long
explanation: Without a passenger's own choice, the rules require the shortest and most direct route to the named destination.

question: An expressway route is longer but likely faster. What should you do?
optionA: Offer it; let the passenger choose
optionB: Take it without asking
optionD: Take it and switch off the meter
explanation: Explaining the choice avoids a later dispute about the route and the fare.

question: A passenger gives only a building name. What is the quickest way to pin down the address?
optionA: Drive to the nearest MRT station and ask
optionB: Guess from the district name
optionC: Ask the passenger to direct every turn
explanation: A six-digit postal code identifies a single building in Singapore and removes doubt between similar names.

question: How many digits does a Singapore postal code have?
optionA: Four
optionB: Six
explanation: Every Singapore address has a six-digit postal code; the first two digits show the postal sector.

question: What do the first two digits of a Singapore postal code show?
optionA: The block's floor count
optionB: The planning year
explanation: The first two digits give the postal sector, which tells you roughly which part of the island the address is in.

question: Which expressway links the Woodlands Causeway area with the PIE?
optionA: Bukit Timah Expressway (BKE)
optionB: East Coast Parkway (ECP)
explanation: The BKE runs from the PIE near Bukit Timah north to Woodlands and the Causeway.

question: Which expressway runs along the east coast between Changi Airport and the city?
optionA: Seletar Expressway (SLE)
optionB: Kranji Expressway (KJE)
explanation: The ECP links Changi Airport with Marina Bay and the city along the southeast coast.

question: Which expressway crosses Singapore from Tuas in the west to Changi in the east?
optionA: Ayer Rajah Expressway (AYE)
optionB: Central Expressway (CTE)
explanation: The PIE is the longest expressway, running east to west across the island from Changi to Tuas.

question: Which expressway runs north from the city centre towards Ang Mo Kio and Seletar?
optionA: Ayer Rajah Expressway (AYE)
optionB: East Coast Parkway (ECP)
explanation: The CTE links the city centre with the north, meeting the SLE and TPE at its northern end.

question: Which expressway links the AYE with the ECP, partly under the sea?
optionA: Kallang-Paya Lebar Expressway (KPE)
optionB: Pan Island Expressway (PIE)
explanation: The MCE connects the AYE and the ECP around Marina South, with a section in an undersea tunnel.

question: Which expressway would you normally use from the city towards the Tuas Second Link to Malaysia?
optionA: Tampines Expressway (TPE)
optionB: Central Expressway (CTE)
explanation: The AYE runs west from the city along the south side of the island to Tuas and the Second Link.

question: Which expressway runs mostly underground between the ECP area and the TPE?
optionA: Kallang-Paya Lebar Expressway (KPE)
optionB: Bukit Timah Expressway (BKE)
explanation: The KPE links the ECP and MCE with the TPE in the northeast, much of it in tunnels.

question: Which expressway links the PIE in the west with the BKE near Bukit Panjang?
optionA: Seletar Expressway (SLE)
optionB: Kranji Expressway (KJE)
explanation: The KJE connects the PIE near Jurong with the BKE.

question: Which expressway links Tampines and Pasir Ris with the SLE in the north?
optionA: Pan Island Expressway (PIE)
optionB: Ayer Rajah Expressway (AYE)
explanation: The TPE runs from the PIE near Tampines towards Sengkang and on to the SLE.

question: On a street directory map, what does a grid reference help you find?
optionA: The speed limit on the road
optionB: The fare to reach the road
explanation: The map number and grid letters and numbers point to the square on the page where the road or building lies.

question: Your navigation app suggests a route through a road you know is closed for works. What should you do?
optionA: Follow the app regardless of the closure
optionB: Stop and wait for the road to open
optionC: Ask the passenger to get out
explanation: Apps are a tool, not a rule. Combine them with what you know and with live traffic news.

question: Why should you check traffic news before a long airport trip at peak hour?
optionA: To raise the fare
optionB: To avoid the worst jams
optionC: To find a cheaper petrol station on the way
explanation: Accidents and jams change the best route. A quick check helps you get the passenger there on time.

question: A large condominium has several blocks and two entrances. What helps most at drop-off?
optionA: Drop them at the main road outside
optionB: Which block and entrance
optionC: Stop at the guardhouse every time
optionD: Choose the entrance nearest the exit
explanation: Confirming the block and entrance saves the passenger a long walk and avoids circling.

question: Your phone loses its signal in a tunnel. What should you rely on?
optionA: Your planned route and signs
optionB: Stopping in the tunnel to reload the map
explanation: Know your exit before entering a tunnel and follow the overhead signs; never stop in a tunnel unless there is an emergency.

question: A passenger asks for a route that avoids an ERP gantry. What should you do?
optionA: Plan a reasonable route avoiding it
optionB: Refuse, as ERP routes are compulsory
optionC: Drive through it and charge more
explanation: The passenger may choose the route. Confirm the alternative so there is no dispute about time or fare.
